replies.body: We should consider whether this method is useful to end users. If not, which I believe is the case here,  instead of adding public api for it we could call it through an internal api. See https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-java-instrumentation/blob/main/instrumentation/runtime-telemetry/library/src/main/java/io/opentelemetry/instrumentation/runtimetelemetry/internal/Internal.java for ideas. Basically you make this method private and register a callback in `Internal` class where you have the a public method that ends up calling this method via the callback. This way this method becomes an internal implemenation detail and we can skip the discussion about whether `List<Map<String, Object>>` makes sense or should be replaced with something else.

The only use-case I see for this method to be public is when we want to add declarative config support in jmx-scraper without having to rely on internal APIs.

- having the jmx-scraper rely on internal APIs is fine as a short-term implementation detail
- we can always promote to the public API if needed, deprecating/replacing is harder

Public API will be useful in custom agents that provide additional sources of JMX rules configuration.
Surely, it can be handled with internal API as well, however it is not so clean IMHO.

My advice would be to go with the internal api. It is hard to justify a public api that accepts `Map<String, Object>`. At minimum there would need to be an explanation what this map contains. I don't think just saying that whatever snakeyaml returns while parsing the yaml is enough. Then there would be a natural question why not make the api accept something structured like some sort of rule object instead of a map. But that is not what you need, the only usage of this api really passes it yaml turned to map. Even if you push for public api it is likely that it will end up being something else than what you need.

threads.body: [for reviewer] The inline list is treated as one configuration source. A parsing failure stops further parsing but keeps already processed rules. Bundled metrics and valid file rules are processed independently.
[for reviewer] The invalid inline rule's unsupported metric type must prevent `custom.test.invalid-inline` from being emitted, while bundled metrics and the valid file rule continue working.

[Config] This non-empty map example is passed to `DeclarativeConfigYamlGenerator.formatValue()`, which only handles empty maps and otherwise uses `String.valueOf`. The generated configuration reference therefore renders `mapping: {ThreadCount={metric=app.thread.count, ...}}` using Java map syntax rather than YAML, so users cannot copy the example to define a working rule. Please extend the generator to serialize nested map examples as YAML and cover this schema with a regression test.

replies.body:
I think in most cases client classes will operate on rules collection anyway, but if you think it is worth changing I can do that.
New method signature should have a singular form then:
`addRule(Map<String, Object> rule)`

There is one issue with this approach.
If declarative config has few rules inlined, and first few are valid, but then there is an invalid rule, then we are unable to discard already added rules. We can no longer satisfy "all or nothing" contract.
What do you think about it?

That's a fair point.

Do we really need to have the 'all or nothing' behavior ?

I don't think it was an explicit requirement or an issue, this is probably implicit with the current implementation where we parse first then add all the created metrics definitions after.
Yes, it is just a convention. I'm OK with processing only a valid metric definitions, log and just skip invalid.

threads.body: A malformed inline rule aborts this stream, so every valid rule after it is skipped. Putting the `type: invalid` rule first therefore prevents otherwise valid thread metrics from being registered. Catch parsing failures per rule so later definitions still load, and cover an invalid rule followed by a valid one.
